intro: SRT to VTT turns SubRip subtitles (.srt) into WebVTT (.vtt), the format the HTML5 <track> element requires to show subtitles on a website's videos, and the one used by YouTube, Vimeo, most web players and many online course platforms.

Each subtitle keeps its timings, to the millisecond, and its line breaks. Italics, bold, underline and strikethrough from the SRT are written with WebVTT tags, and special characters such as “&” or “<” are escaped as the format requires, so the browser does not mistake them for tags. If you prefer, you can drop the styling and keep plain text.

The conversion runs on our server: subtitles are read with pysubs2, a widely used free library for this job, and the new file is written in UTF-8 and sorted by time. We detect the original's encoding, so old subtitles in Windows-1252, with all their accents, come out right. You can convert up to 20 files at once and download them together in a ZIP.
On the page, add the file to the video with <track kind="subtitles" src="subtitles.vtt" srclang="en" label="English">. The server has to deliver the .vtt with the text/vtt type; most already do.
steps: Choose whether to keep the text styling.

faq.a: This tool copies the timings as they are. To translate subtitles into another language, use Translate subtitles.

faq.q: Why did my SRT have colours and now it doesn't?
faq.a: The <font color> tags some SRT files use are not standard and are not kept. In WebVTT, colours are set with CSS on the page.
VTT to SRT turns WebVTT into SRT for desktop players and video editors.
